newsitem.title: FRANCE: French watchdog reports on scandal-prone phonetaps.
newsitem.headline: French watchdog reports on scandal-prone phonetaps.

text.p: France's watchdog on phone-tapping, a practice at the heart of a scandal darkening the late President Francois Mitterrand's legacy, hands its annual report to Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Tuesday.
The National Commission for Control of Intercepts and Security (CNCIS) publishes its findings at five p.m. (1600 GMT), only days after fresh revelations of wire-tapping under Mitterrand.

Files of Mitterrand's former anti-terrorist cell, extracts of which were published by the media, show he personally oversaw widespread illegal taps of journalists, lawyers and politicians. Many papers carried his laconic handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).

The CNCIS, which the government must consult on all its requests for telepone taps, will detail how many were carried out last year against 1995's total of more than 4,000, and when, if at all, Juppe overrode its advice.
Under a 1991 law, phone taps can be carried out only on grounds of national security, safeguarding economic or scientific interests, and the fight against crime or terrorism.
Officials said commission president Paul Bouchet may also make policy recommendations. Last year he denounced clandestine telephone taps by private groups, estimated at some 100,000.

Under a bill to be debated by the Senate next month, the maximum sentence for illegal taps would be doubled to two years. The commission would also be given the task of monitoring companies using or trading in equipment which could be used for taps.
Bouchet was this week directed to study documents from Mitterrand's since-disbanded cell that were seized by France's DST counter-intelligence service last month on national security grounds.

He will report back to Juppe within a few weeks on whether their seizure was justified. If not, certain documents may be passed on to investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat who is probing the illegal wiretaps.
A senior aide to Mitterrand told Valat last week he was prepared to breach official secrecy to answer questions about the wiretapping under the former Socialist leader.
Gilles Menage, former head of Mitterrand's private office, is under investigation for allegedly authorising the anti-terrorism unit to carry out widespread illegal wiretapping from 1982 to 1986.
He told reporters he had named a first list of 10 to 15 people on whom he was prepared to explain the grounds for wiretapping, out of 150 for which he is being investigated.
Among them he cited investigative journalist Edwy Plenel of the newspaper Le Monde, lawyer Antoine Comte and writer Jean-Edern Hallier, who died recently.

In an apparent attempt to shield France's present conservative rulers, Menage said he would not reveal secrets involving the 1986-1988 "cohabitation" period when conservative President Jacques Chirac was Mitterrand's prime minister.
French media have reported that up to 2,000 people were victims of wiretapping by the Elysee palace unit. The daily Liberation said some 100,000 people were being illegally wiretapped each year.
Mitterrand, who served from 1981 to 1995, died last year of prostate cancer just eight months after leaving office.
